instagram_reel.hook: Pinot Noir is basically the wine world’s drama queen — and I mean that in the best way.
instagram_reel.script:
Pinot Noir has a big reputation for a reason. It’s a thin-skinned red grape, which means it’s sensitive, tricky, and very honest. It does not hide where it’s from.

That’s why people love it. When Pinot Noir is good, it can be so beautiful — lighter in colour, bright red fruit, good acidity, softer tannins. And with age, you start getting those earthy, savoury notes people chase.

It’s grown in Burgundy, of course, but also in places like Oregon, California, New Zealand, and right here in Ontario. And yes, it even shows up in Champagne and rosé.

So if Pinot Noir has ever felt a little mysterious, that’s the point. It asks for more — and usually gives more back.

tiktok.hook: Why does Pinot Noir get all this attention? Because it’s beautiful... and a little difficult.
tiktok.script:
Pinot Noir has a whole mythology around it, and honestly, it deserves some of it. This is a thin-skinned red grape, so it’s sensitive and tricky to grow. It shows everything — the vineyard, the climate, the winemaking.

That’s why people say it’s one of the purest expressions of place. In the glass, it’s usually lighter, with red fruit like cherry and raspberry, bright acidity, and softer tannins.

And while Burgundy is the classic home, Pinot Noir also shines in Oregon, California, New Zealand, and Ontario. It’s even one of the key grapes in Champagne.

So yeah — demanding grape, but when it hits, it really hits.

linkedin.post:
Pinot Noir has earned its reputation as one of the most compelling grapes in wine.

It is delicate, expressive, and highly sensitive to site, climate, and winemaking decisions. That sensitivity is also what makes it such a strong example of terroir — it tells you where it comes from.

From Burgundy’s layered classification system to cool-climate regions like Oregon, New Zealand, California’s coastal zones, and Ontario’s Niagara Peninsula, Pinot Noir continues to reward producers who are willing to work carefully with it.

What makes it especially interesting from an industry perspective is its versatility: it is central to still red wine, but it also plays an important role in Champagne and rosé production.

For consumers and trade alike, Pinot Noir remains a benchmark grape — demanding, yes, but capable of remarkable nuance and value at every level.
